title: Week 7 Greedy Drill
h1: Greedy, interval scheduling, Prim and Kruskal drill
footer: Written from the Week 7 lecture and lab. New activities and a new graph, not the practice quiz. The Prim and Kruskal traces were checked in Python.

qs.p: Coins are worth 1, 5 and 6. You must pay 10 with as few coins as possible. Greedy always takes the biggest coin that fits. How many coins does greedy use, and how many does the best answer use?
qs.ex: Greedy: 6, then 1, 1, 1, 1, which is 5 coins. Best: 5 and 5, which is 2 coins. This shows greedy is not always optimal.

qs.p: Activities: A [1, 3), B [2, 5), C [4, 7), D [6, 9), E [8, 10), F [3, 4). Which activities does the earliest finish time greedy algorithm pick?
qs.ex: Sort by finish: A (3), F (4), B (5), C (7), D (9), E (10). Pick A, last finish 3. F starts at 3, which is at or after 3, so pick it, last finish 4. B starts at 2, skip. C starts at 4, pick, last finish 7. D starts at 6, skip. E starts at 8, pick. Result A, F, C, E. Option A forgets that F may start exactly when A finishes.

qs.p: For interval scheduling, which ordering rule ALWAYS gives the largest set of non-overlapping activities?
qs.ex: Only earliest finish time is always optimal. Earliest start fails when one long activity starts first, for example [0, 10) blocks [1, 2), [2, 3) and [3, 4). Shortest and fewest conflicts also have counterexamples.

qs.p: What is the running time of the earliest finish time algorithm on n activities that are not sorted?
qs.ex: Sorting by finish time costs O(n log n), and the scan after it is O(n). Sorting dominates. O(n) is only when the input is already sorted. O(2ⁿ) is trying every subset.

qs.p: Which two properties must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be correct?
opts: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
A sorted input and a base case
qs.ex: Greedy choice property: some best answer contains the greedy choice. Optimal substructure: after the choice, the rest is a best answer to the smaller problem. Overlapping subproblems is what DP needs.

sections.label: Section 2
sections.name: MSTs and Prim's algorithm
sections.figcap: Use this undirected graph for sections 2 and 3.

qs.p: Run Prim's algorithm from A. In what order are the vertices added to the tree?
opts: A, B, C, D, E, F, G
A, C, D, B, E, F, G
A, C, B, D, E, G, F
A, C, B, D, E, F, G
qs.ex: Start A. Crossing edges A–B 4, A–C 1: add C. Now A–B 4, C–B 3, C–D 5, C–E 7: add B (3). Now B–D 2: add D. Now D–E 6, C–E 7, D–F 9: add E (6). Now E–F 8, D–F 9, E–G 10: add F (8). Last E–G 10, F–G 11: add G. Order A, C, B, D, E, F, G.

qs.p: What is the total weight of the minimum spanning tree?
qs.ex: MST edges: A–C 1, B–D 2, B–C 3, D–E 6, E–F 8, E–G 10. Total 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 30.

qs.p: Split the vertices into {A, B, C} and {D, E, F, G}. By the cut property, which edge must be in every MST?
qs.ex: The edges crossing between the groups are B–D 2, C–D 5 and C–E 7. The lightest crossing edge is B–D (2). A–C does not cross: both ends are in {A, B, C}.

qs.p: This graph has 7 vertices and 11 edges. How many edges does any spanning tree of it have?
qs.ex: A spanning tree on V vertices always has V − 1 edges: 7 − 1 = 6.

qs.p: What is the running time of Prim's algorithm with an adjacency list and a binary heap?
qs.ex: Each edge goes into the heap at most once and each heap step costs O(log), giving O(E log V). With an adjacency matrix and a simple search for the minimum it is O(V²).

qs.p: Run Kruskal's algorithm on the same graph. Which is the THIRD edge accepted?
qs.ex: Sorted: A–C 1 accept, B–D 2 accept, B–C 3 accept (B and C are in different groups). So the third accepted edge is B–C.

qs.p: Which is the FIRST edge that Kruskal's algorithm rejects?
qs.ex: After A–C, B–D and B–C, the group {A, B, C, D} is joined. A–B (4) is next, and A and B are already connected through C, so it would make a cycle: reject. C–D (5) is rejected too, but later.

qs.p: The edges D–E (6), E–F (8) and D–F (9) form a cycle. By the cycle property, which edge is in NO minimum spanning tree?
qs.ex: The heaviest edge on a cycle is never in an MST (when weights are different). The heaviest here is D–F (9). Kruskal rejects it for the same reason: D and F are already joined.

qs.p: What is the running time of Kruskal's algorithm using a disjoint set forest (union-find)?
qs.ex: Sorting the E edges costs O(E log E), which is the same as O(E log V), and union-find makes each merge almost free, so sorting dominates. With a simple label array the merges add O(V²).
